payload.markdown:
Malay uses the same 26 letters you already read. The trap is that it uses them differently. English **e** has several sounds; Malay **e** has two. English **c** is sometimes *k*, sometimes *s*; Malay **c** is always the *ch* in *church*. Read *terima kasih* with English vowel rules and you get "teh-RYE-mah KAY-see" — nobody in a mamak will turn around. Read it with the table below and you get "tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh", which works.

Two rules carry most of the load.

**Vowels are short and pure.** *a* is the *a* in *father*, *i* is *ee* in *see*, *u* is *oo* in *food*, *o* is *o* in *low* with no *w* sliding off the end. No diphthongs — do not glide.

**Consonants are single-valued.** *c* is always *ch*. *g* is always hard, as in *go* — never the soft *g* of *giant*. *j* is the *j* in *jug*. *ng* is the *ng* in *singer*, with no hard *g* after it; *ngg* is the *ng* in *finger*, with one. *ny* is the *ny* in *canyon*. *sy* is *sh*. *kh* is the Scottish *ch* in *loch*.

Two endings need practice. A word-final **-a** softens to a short *uh* in everyday Peninsular speech: *saya* is "sa-yuh", not "sa-yah". And a word-final **-k** is not a *k* at all — it is a stop in the throat, the sound you make in the middle of "uh-oh". *tidak* comes out "tida'" with the mouth closing and nothing released.

Stress is light and even. Most speakers lean slightly on the second-last syllable, but leaning wrong costs you far less than mispronouncing a *c* or a final *a*.

blocks.title: Reading terima kasih off the table

payload.title: Reading terima kasih off the table
payload.markdown:
Your phrasebook lists *terima kasih* (thank you). Here is the whole word taken apart with the table, letter group by letter group.

| Chunk | Letters | Rule | Sound |
|---|---|---|---|
| te- | t, e | **e** is the short *uh* of *about* | tuh |
| -ri- | r, i | **r** tapped; **i** is *ee* in *see* | ree |
| -ma | m, a | **a** is *a* in *father*; it ends the word *terima*, so in relaxed speech it may soften to *uh* | mah |
| ka- | k, a | same **a** | kah |
| -sih | s, i, h | **i** is *ee*; final **h** is breathed | seeh |

Put together: **tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh**. Stress sits lightly on the second-last syllable of each word — *tuh-REE-mah*, *KAH-seeh*.

Now the same method on a word you will meet at the counter. *ais* (iced) is not English "ace": **a** is *a* in *father*, **i** is *ee*, so it is "ah-ees", two syllables, not one. And *kopi* is "ko-pee", not "KOH-pye".

Run the method on any new word: split it, apply the table to each chunk, then check the two endings — a final **-a** softens, a final **-k** stops.

lessons.title: Greeting people, introducing yourself, what to call them
lessons.summary: You will be able to greet someone, thank them, apologise and introduce yourself as an international student at Taylor's. Covers Helo and Selamat pagi, terima kasih, maaf, saya against aku, anda against awak, and the kinship words pakcik, makcik, abang and kakak. Prevents calling a man old enough to be your father awak.

payload.markdown:
You are standing at the counter of a mamak at 8am. The man behind it is roughly your father's age. You open your mouth and out comes *awak* — the word you drilled last night for "you". His face does not change, but the transaction does: he answers you in English for the rest of the order, and you have just told him, in his own language, that the two of you are peers.

Malay has two systems running side by side, and the one you pick is a social decision, not a grammar decision.

**The neutral set** is what a stranger uses. *Saya* for I, *awak* for you when you are clearly the same age or younger, *anda* for you on signs, forms and in formal writing. For a stranger you cannot place, use a title instead of "you": *Encik* (any adult man), *Puan* (a married or older woman), *Cik* (a young woman). These are the words in your phrasebook table, and they are safe because they carry no claim about the relationship.

**The kinship set** is what Malaysians actually reach for. *Pak cik* (uncle) for a man old enough to be your father, *mak cik* (auntie) for a woman the same, *abang* (older brother) for a man a few years older, *kakak* (older sister) for a woman a few years older. These are not literal family. A mamak uncle is a *pak cik* on first meeting. The Grab driver who is 30 is an *abang*. The woman at the campus counter is a *kakak*.

The rule that keeps you out of trouble: **when you can see the person, kinship beats pronoun.** *Awak* is for someone you have already established as a peer — a classmate, someone your age who has introduced themselves. Used on a *pak cik*, it reads as a demotion. Used on a *kakak* at the faculty office, it reads as a student who has not learned where they are.

The phrasebook table in section 2 of your phrasebook gives you *Siapa nama awak?* and *Nama saya Oybek.* — note that the model sentence uses *awak*, because it is written for peer-to-peer introductions. When you introduce yourself to a *pak cik*, you swap the pronoun for the kinship word and the rest of the sentence does not move: *Siapa nama pak cik?* / *Nama saya Oybek.*

Greetings layer on top of this. *Selamat pagi* until about noon, *selamat tengah hari* around midday, *selamat petang* from mid-afternoon until dusk, *selamat malam* after dark. *Helo* works at any hour and carries no religious weight. *Assalamualaikum* is the Muslim greeting you will hear often; the reply is *Waalaikumussalam*. If you are unsure, *Helo* is never wrong.

Two more words do more work than their length suggests. *Terima kasih* is thank you; *terima kasih banyak* is thank you very much, and it is what you say to a *pak cik* who has just walked your order to the table. *Maaf* covers both sorry and excuse me; *minta maaf* is the fuller apology you use when you have actually done something — knocked a drink over, arrived late to a tutorial.

blocks.title: Ordering at a mamak, three ways

payload.title: Ordering at a mamak, three ways
payload.markdown:
The same transaction, run three times. The only thing that changes is the word for "you".

**Setup.** It is 8:15am. The stall is run by a man in his fifties. You want *roti canai* and *teh tarik*. You have learned *Siapa nama awak?* and *Nama saya Oybek.* from section 2 of your phrasebook.

**Attempt 1 — the phrasebook sentence, unchanged.**
> You: *Selamat pagi. Siapa nama awak?*
>
> Pak cik: *Selamat pagi. [in English] What would you like?*

He answered the greeting in Malay and the question in English. *Awak* told him you were addressing him as a peer, and he corrected the register by switching languages. Nothing rude happened, but you lost the exchange.

**Attempt 2 — kinship swapped in.**
> You: *Selamat pagi, pak cik. Siapa nama pak cik?*
>
> Pak cik: *Selamat pagi. [name]. Nak apa?*

*Nak apa?* is "what do you want?" — the standard next move. You have been read as a polite student, and he is now speaking Malay to you.

**Attempt 3 — the full order.**
> You: *Selamat pagi, pak cik. Saya nak roti canai satu, teh tarik satu.*
>
> Pak cik: *Boleh.*
>
> *(food arrives)*
>
> You: *Terima kasih banyak, pak cik.*
>
> Pak cik: *Sama-sama.*

**What changed between 1 and 3.** Not vocabulary — you used *selamat pagi* and *terima kasih* in all three. The single substitution of *awak* → *pak cik* is what moved the conversation from English back into Malay, and *terima kasih banyak* rather than plain *terima kasih* is what closes it. Note also that *saya* never changes: it is safe in every one of the three attempts. The pronoun that carries risk is the one for the other person, not the one for you.

payload.why_it_seems_right: It is the word your phrasebook table puts in the model sentence *Siapa nama awak?*, and phrasebook model sentences are usually the safe default. It also sounds softer than *anda*, which reads like a form, so it feels like the friendlier choice.
payload.what_is_true: *Awak* is the peer word, not the polite word. It asserts that you and the person you are addressing are on the same level, and it is the correct default only for someone your own age. Addressing a *pak cik* — a man old enough to be your father — as *awak* is not a grammar error, it is a social one: you have claimed equality with him. The phrasebook's model sentence is written for peer-to-peer introductions, which is why it uses *awak*; the moment the person in front of you is a generation older, the sentence stays and the pronoun swaps to *pak cik*. The difference predicts the response: use *awak* on a mamak uncle and he answers in English; use *pak cik* and he keeps speaking Malay.

steps.prompt: You reach the counter. He looks up. What comes out of your mouth first?

options.outcome_markdown: He nods and says *Selamat pagi* back. He is still speaking Malay. You have been read as a polite student and the transaction is running in the language you wanted.
He pauses for half a second, then answers in English: *Good morning, what would you like?* Nothing rude happened, but the conversation has left Malay and will not come back.
He says *Helo* back and waits. It is not wrong — *helo* is never wrong — but it gave him no signal about register, so he defaults to English.

steps.prompt: He asks *Nak apa?* You want to order. Which sentence?

options.text: Saya nak roti canai satu, teh tarik satu.
options.outcome_markdown: He says *Boleh* and turns to the griddle. The order is in. *Saya* is the same word you would use with anyone.
He stops. *Awak nak* means "you want" — you have just told him what he wants. He repeats the question slowly, in English, to check.
He switches to English and takes the order that way. You got your food, and you spent the one Malay exchange you had this morning.

steps.prompt: The food arrives. He sets it down. What do you say?

options.outcome_markdown: He says *Sama-sama* and moves on. You have closed the exchange in Malay, which is what makes him remember you tomorrow.
He looks amused: *sama-sama* is the reply to a thank-you ("you're welcome"), not the thank-you itself. That is his line, not yours.
He looks up, puzzled — you have just apologised for something he cannot identify. *Minta maaf* is for when you have actually done something wrong.

payload.debrief_markdown: Every wrong turn in this scenario was the same mistake in a different costume: reaching for a word that carries no information about the relationship. *Awak* and *helo* both leave the register blank, and a stranger fills a blank with the safest option available to them — usually English. *Pak cik* is the one word that tells him who you think he is, and it is the word that keeps the conversation in Malay. Notice also that *saya* never had to change. The risk lives entirely in the word for the other person.

lessons.title: Numbers, money and telling the time
lessons.summary: You will be able to hear a price, count past a hundred, read a clock time and agree a day with someone. Covers satu to sepuluh, the -belas teens like sebelas, the puluh tens, kosong for the zero in phone numbers, ringgit and sen, and sekarang, hari ini, esok, pagi, petang and malam. Prevents nodding at lapan ringgit when the number you actually heard was lapan puluh.

payload.markdown:
You are at a mamak table. The waiter says **lapan ringgit**. You hear *lapan* and hand over RM 8. He waits. The bill was **lapan puluh** — eighty. That RM 72 gap is the whole reason this lesson exists.

Malay numbers are built from a small set of parts, and the parts are regular. Learn the ten digits and you can say any price up to 999 without new vocabulary.

| Digit | Malay |
|---|---|
| 0 | sifar (kosong for phone numbers) |
| 1 | satu |
| 2 | dua |
| 3 | tiga |
| 4 | empat |
| 5 | lima |
| 6 | enam |
| 7 | tujuh |
| 8 | lapan |
| 9 | sembilan |
| 10 | sepuluh |

Three rules generate everything else.

**Teens add *belas*.** 11 is *sebelas* (the *se-* swallows the *satu*), then 12 *dua belas*, 13 *tiga belas*, up to 19 *sembilan belas*.

**Tens add *puluh*.** 20 is *dua puluh*, 30 *tiga puluh*, 50 *lima puluh*. Units come after: 21 is *dua puluh satu*, 45 is *empat puluh lima*, 99 is *sembilan puluh sembilan*.

**One hundred and one thousand take *se-*, not *satu*.** 100 is *seratus*, 1000 is *seribu*, 1,000,000 is *sejuta*. But 200 is *dua ratus* and 2000 is *dua ribu*.

So RM 87 is *lapan puluh tujuh ringgit*. RM 8 is *lapan ringgit*. The difference between them is one word, and it is the word you must not drop.

Money: RM is *ringgit*, and 1 ringgit = 100 sen. RM 4.50 is *empat ringgit lima puluh sen*. In a shop you will hear *kosong* for the zero in a phone number or a digit string — 012 reads *kosong satu dua*.

Time is the same arithmetic. *Pukul berapa sekarang?* asks the time. *Pukul satu* is one o'clock, *pukul dua setengah* is half past two — *setengah* after the hour means half past, not half to. Days: Isnin, Selasa, Rabu, Khamis, Jumaat, Sabtu, Ahad. *Hari ini* is today, *esok* tomorrow, *semalam* yesterday. *Pagi* is morning, *tengah hari* midday, *petang* afternoon to dusk, *malam* night.

options.text: Say *Lapan ringgit?* to check, then hand over the RM 10 note.

lessons.title: Ordering at the mamak: drinks, food, paying
lessons.summary: You will be able to sit down at a mamak, order drinks and food, and settle the bill. Covers teh and teh tarik, teh o and kosong, kopi, kurang manis, the roti and rice dishes you will actually meet, and berapa and bungkus for the price and for takeaway. Prevents surprise at the drink that arrives with condensed milk in it, because teh is the default and not plain tea.

payload.markdown:
You sit down at a mamak. The waiter arrives in about eight seconds and asks **"Nak minum apa?"** — what do you want to drink. If you say *teh*, you get hot tea with condensed milk in it. Sweet, milky, and nothing like the plain tea you were picturing.

That is the whole problem this lesson solves. At a mamak the default is sweet and milky, and you have to say extra words to get anything else.

Your phrasebook (section 5, "At the mamak") lays out the drink grid. Read it as three switches, not a list of drinks:

| Switch | Setting | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Milk | *teh* / *kopi* | condensed milk in |
| Milk | *teh O* / *kopi O* | "O" means no milk, sugar stays |
| Sugar | (nothing) | full sugar |
| Sugar | *kurang manis* | less sweet |
| Sugar | *kosong* | no sugar |
| Temperature | (nothing) | hot |
| Temperature | *ais* | iced |

So *teh O kosong* is black tea, no milk, no sugar. *Teh tarik* is the same milk tea pulled between two cups until it froths — same drink, more air, and it is what the phrasebook's own dialogue has you order. *Milo ais* is iced Milo, no switches needed.

Food works the same way. *Roti canai* is flaky flatbread with curry; *roti kosong* is that bread plain — here *kosong* means plain, not sugarless, because the word is doing its real job: "nothing added". *Roti telur* has egg cooked into it. *Nasi lemak* is coconut rice with sambal, anchovies, peanuts and egg. *Mee goreng mamak* is mamak fried noodles. *Kuah campur* is mixed curry gravy, and it is how you ask for more than one curry on the plate.

Two more words finish the meal. **Bungkus** means takeaway — *tapau* means the same thing and comes from Cantonese, so both work. **Bang** is how you address the waiter; the phrasebook's dialogue ends with *"Terima kasih, bang!"*.

And when you are done: **"Bang, kira."** That is the bill. Not a question, just the request.

payload.title: Four orders, four different cups
payload.markdown:
You are at a mamak near campus. Same table, four different days.

**Day 1.** You say *"Teh satu."* The waiter writes it down. What arrives: hot tea with condensed milk, full sugar. You did not ask for milk. The default put it there.

**Day 2.** You say *"Teh O satu."* What arrives: hot tea, no milk, sugar still in. The *O* removed exactly one thing.

**Day 3.** You say *"Teh O kosong satu."* What arrives: hot black tea, nothing added. Two switches, two words.

**Day 4.** You say *"Teh tarik kurang manis, satu."* — the phrasebook's own dialogue line. What arrives: hot pulled milk tea, less sugar than normal. The milk is still there; *kurang manis* only touched the sugar.

Now the food side, same table:

> **Waiter:** Makan? *(Anything to eat?)*
>
> **You:** Roti canai satu, kuah campur.

The *satu* goes after the dish, the way the phrasebook's dialogue says it. *Kuah campur* gets you mixed curry rather than one. If you had said *roti kosong* you would get the same bread with no egg and no filling — plain.

You eat. Then:

> **You:** Bang, kira.
>
> **Waiter:** Empat ringgit lima puluh sen. *(RM 4.50.)*

That price is the phrasebook's, from the dialogue in section 5. You already know *empat ringgit lima puluh sen* from the numbers and money lesson, so the bill is not a surprise — you can hear it and pay it.

If you were taking it home instead of eating there, you would have said *bungkus* when ordering, or *tapau*. Same meaning, different word.

payload.belief: The word teh just means tea, so if I order teh I get a plain cup of hot tea like at home.
payload.why_it_seems_right: The word maps cleanly onto English "tea", and every other drink name you know works that way — you say "coffee" and you get coffee, black, and you add what you want yourself. Nothing in the word "teh" warns you that milk and sugar are already in it.
payload.what_is_true: At a mamak, teh is the default milk tea: hot tea with condensed milk and sugar already in the cup. Your phrasebook's mamak table gives it as "hot tea with condensed milk (the default)". To get anything else you add words — teh O removes the milk, kosong removes the sugar, ais makes it cold. The same default logic runs through the food: roti kosong is plain roti, because kosong means "nothing added", not "no sugar". payload.setup_markdown: It is your third day in Malaysia. You are at the mamak two streets from Taylor's with two friends. You have RM 20 in your pocket. You are thirsty, you have not eaten since breakfast, and you have a 2pm class.

steps.prompt: The waiter arrives and asks "Nak minum apa?" You want something cold, and you have already had two sweet drinks today. What do you say?

options.outcome_markdown: A tall glass of iced milk tea arrives, dark and sweet. You drink it, but it is the third sweet drink of the day and you are still thirsty afterwards.
A tall glass of iced tea arrives with no milk and no sugar. Cold, clean, and exactly what you asked for.
A glass of warm water arrives. It is fine, but it is not what you wanted and you will be ordering again in ten minutes.

steps.prompt: Drinks are down. The waiter asks "Makan?" You want flatbread with egg cooked into it, and mixed curry. What do you order?

options.outcome_markdown: Plain roti arrives with mixed curry. Tasty, but there is no egg: *kosong* means nothing added.
Roti with egg cooked into it arrives, with mixed curry gravy. You eat it with your hands, the way the table next to you is doing.
Coconut rice with sambal, anchovies, peanuts and egg arrives, and the sambal is mild as asked. Good, but this is a rice dish, not the egg roti you were after.

steps.prompt: You have eaten and you need to get to your 2pm class. What do you say to the waiter?

options.outcome_markdown: The waiter brings the bill and says the total out loud. You count out the ringgit, leave it on the table, and you are out the door with time to spare.
Another of whatever you last ordered arrives. You now have more food than you can finish and less time before class.
The waiter smiles and walks off to another table. You sit there with an unpaid bill until you catch his eye again.

payload.debrief_markdown: Every wrong turn in this scenario is the same mistake: saying something true and polite instead of saying the specific thing you want. "Teh ais" is a real order, just not the one you wanted. "Roti kosong" is real food, just without the egg. "Terima kasih" is real gratitude, just not a request for the bill. At a mamak the waiter is not going to interview you — he writes down what you say and walks away. The words that do the work are the modifiers: O, kosong, kurang manis, ais, campur, bungkus. Learn the modifiers and the drink names become a grid you can steer instead of a lottery you draw from.

lessons.title: Grab, directions and getting to campus
lessons.summary: You will be able to book a Grab, tell the driver where you are going and ask your way on foot. Covers Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus, Abang dah sampai? when the car is not where you are standing, and kiri, kanan and terus on campus. Prevents the silent ride where neither of you is sure the other has understood.

payload.markdown:
The Grab arrives. You get in. Neither of you says anything useful for eleven minutes, and you spend the whole ride hoping the pin was right.

That silence is the thing this lesson removes. It is not a vocabulary problem — you already know enough words. It is a *sequencing* problem: the ride has four moments where something must be said, and if you say them in the wrong order or skip one, the driver fills the gap with his own guess.

The four moments, in order:

1. **When he calls or texts** — tell him where you are standing, in a way he can act on.
2. **Before he moves** — confirm the destination out loud, even though the app already shows it. This is your best chance to catch a wrong pin while the car is still stationary.
3. **While moving** — give directions only if he asks or if he is clearly about to miss the turn.
4. **On arrival** — stop him at the right gate, not at the security post 400 metres earlier.

Your source phrasebook has all of these in section 6. What it does not give you is the order, and the order is what stops the silent ride.

Two things about how the words sound, from section 1 of the same phrasebook. Final *k* is a short stop in the throat, not a full "k" — so *tidak* comes out closer to "tida'". And stress is light and fairly even, leaning slightly on the second-last syllable. That matters here because *belok* and *terus* are the two words a driver has to catch over engine noise, and both are short.

One structural note before you start. On campus, the same three direction words do all the work: *kiri*, *kanan*, *terus*. You will use them on foot, in a car, and pointing at a map on someone's phone. Learn them once, here.

payload.intro: The full ride, from booking to getting out, in the order it happens: first the driver has to find you, then you confirm where you are going, then you steer and stop.

steps.title: When he calls, describe where you are standing
steps.detail_markdown:
Drivers often call rather than text. Answer, and say where you are:

> **Saya tunggu di pintu utama.**

Then add one thing he can see from the road:

> **Saya pakai baju biru.**

If you are not there yet:

> **Saya lambat sikit, lima minit.**

Swap *biru* for whatever colour you are actually wearing. The colour is the whole point — it is the only part of this that he can use from a moving car.
steps.warning: Do not say *Saya dah sampai* (I've arrived) if you are not yet at the pickup point: it tells him you are standing there now, and he will look for you there. If you are late, say *Saya lambat sikit, lima minit.*
steps.check: He has stopped describing where he is and started describing where you are. That is the switch you are listening for.

steps.title: Ask whether he has arrived, once, if the car is not where you are
steps.detail_markdown:
If the app says the car is here and you cannot see it, send:

> **Abang dah sampai?**

*Abang* is the friendly address for a man a bit older than you — the same *bang* you use for the mamak waiter. It is the right word for a Grab driver too.

Send it once. If he does not reply within a minute, call. Do not send it three times; a driver who is circling a one-way system cannot read while driving, and repeated messages make him stop reading altogether.
steps.warning: Do not walk toward where you think the car is. Stay at the pin. A moving passenger and a moving driver can circle each other for ten minutes; a stationary passenger gets found.
steps.check: You have a reply, or you have called and spoken. If neither, cancel and rebook — you are past the point where more messages help.

steps.title: Get in and say the destination out loud
steps.detail_markdown:
As you open the door or just after you sit down, say:

> **Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus.**

This is the phrase from section 6 of your phrasebook. You are not asking a question — you are stating the destination so he can confirm it. If he repeats it back or nods, you are aligned. If he says something you do not catch, point at his phone screen and say *ini* while tapping the pin.

Say it before the car moves. A wrong pin corrected at the kerb costs ten seconds; corrected 3 km down the road it costs a fare and an argument.
steps.warning: Do not skip this because the app already shows the destination. A campus has several gates, and a pin dropped at the wrong one still routes somewhere.
steps.check: He has said the destination back, or nodded while looking at his own screen. If neither happened, say it again more slowly.

steps.title: Give directions only when he asks or is about to miss a turn
steps.detail_markdown:
Three words, from section 6:

| Malay | English |
|---|---|
| **Belok kiri.** | Turn left. |
| **Belok kanan.** | Turn right. |
| **Jalan terus.** | Go straight on. |

And if he overshoots:

> **Pusing balik.**

Say the word, then point. The gesture and the word together survive engine noise; either one alone often does not. Your phrasebook notes that Wikivoyage also lists *Pusing kiri* and *Pusing kanan* for left and right — if a driver uses those, they mean the same thing, and *belok* is the safer word to produce yourself.

If he asks how long:

> **Berapa lama?**

is the question, and *Jalan sesak* or *Jem* is what he will say back if the answer is bad.
steps.warning: Do not narrate the whole route. A driver who knows the campus better than you will find constant directions distracting, and you will run out of attention before the turns that matter.
steps.check: He has taken at least one turn you asked for. If he has ignored two, stop giving directions — he knows a route you do not.

steps.title: Stop him at the right gate
steps.detail_markdown:
When you can see where you want to get out:

> **Tolong berhenti di sini.**

Say it early enough that he can pull over legally. On a campus road that means roughly 50 metres before the point you actually want, because he needs to find a gap.

If you are not sure whether you are close enough yet, ask:

> **Dekat atau jauh?**

using *dekat* and *jauh* from the same table.
steps.warning: Do not wait until you are level with the gate. At that point he has already passed the turning and you will be dropped on the far side of a divided road.
steps.check: The car has stopped and he has not asked you for more money than the app quoted.

steps.title: On foot, use the same three words
steps.detail_markdown:
The direction words do not change when you get out of the car. If you are lost on campus and stop someone:

> **Di mana perpustakaan?**

Then listen for *kiri*, *kanan* or *terus* in the answer. Those three are the whole of what you need to catch. If the answer comes too fast, say the place again and point — most people will point as they repeat it, and the point is the answer.

*Di mana perpustakaan?* is from section 7 of your phrasebook; the rest of the campus words come in the campus lesson.
steps.warning: Do not nod at an answer you did not understand. Ask again with the place name — *perpustakaan?* — and let them point. A wrong nod sends you 200 metres in the wrong direction and you will not know until you are there.
steps.check: You can see the building, or the person has pointed at something you can see.

lessons.title: On campus and in your BMK class
lessons.summary: You will be able to introduce yourself to a lecturer, find the library and the admin office, and stop a class from running straight past you. Covers Saya pelajar antarabangsa, Di mana perpustakaan?, Saya tak faham, Boleh ulang? and minta maaf. Prevents sitting through a whole BMK session without ever saying you did not follow.

payload.markdown:
On the Grab ride in you learned to say *Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's*. That gets you to the gate. It does not get you through a lecture.

The gap is not vocabulary. It is that a BMK class moves at the speed of the room, and if you never say anything, the tutor will keep going and you will sit through the whole class understanding nothing. Three phrases stop that:

- **Saya tak faham.** — I don't understand.
- **Boleh ulang?** — Can you repeat that?
- **Boleh cakap perlahan sikit?** — Can you speak a bit slower?

Your phrasebook lists all three in its basics table, and they are the ones that keep a class from running past you. A tutor who hears *Saya tak faham* will rephrase. A tutor who hears nothing assumes you followed.

Two habits make these work. First, **Minta maaf** before the request — it is more polite than plain *maaf*, and you are interrupting. Second, say the phrase even when you half-understood. Half-understanding is the state you are trying to escape, and it looks identical to full understanding from the front of the room.

For the lecturer, one sentence carries the whole introduction: **Saya pelajar antarabangsa.** Add where you are from and what you study and you are done — *Saya dari Uzbekistan. Saya belajar sains komputer.*

For buildings, the pattern is **Di mana** plus the place. *Di mana perpustakaan?* works for the library, the admin office, the toilet. For class timing, **Bila kelas mula?**

And when a word goes past you, do not nod. Ask **Apa maksud "tugasan"?** — *tugasan* is assignment, and it will appear on every brief you get this semester.

payload.intro: How to actually do this in the room. The order matters: you apologise, you name the problem, you make one specific request. Do not stack three requests at once — you will get three answers at speed and be back where you started.

steps.title: Open with Minta maaf
steps.detail_markdown: Raise your hand slightly and say **Minta maaf.** Your phrasebook marks this as more polite than plain *maaf* — you are interrupting a class, so use the polite one.
steps.warning: Do not start with *Saya tak faham* alone. Without the apology it reads as a flat statement of fact rather than a request for help.
steps.check: The tutor's eyes are on you and they have stopped talking.

steps.title: Name the problem in one sentence
steps.detail_markdown: Say **Saya tak faham.** Nothing else. This is the single most useful sentence in the room and it is complete on its own.
steps.warning: Do not add an explanation in English. The moment you switch to English the tutor may switch too, and you lose the practice.
steps.check: The tutor acknowledges you — usually a nod, or *oh, tak faham*.

steps.title: Make one specific request
steps.detail_markdown: Pick exactly one: **Boleh ulang?** if you missed the content, or **Boleh cakap perlahan sikit?** if you heard it but could not keep up. Say it once and stop.
steps.warning: Asking both in a row gets you a fast repeat, which is the original problem.
steps.check: The tutor repeats or slows down, and you catch more the second time.

steps.title: Ask about the one word you missed
steps.detail_markdown: If a single word is the blocker, name it: **Apa maksud "tugasan"?** The pattern is *Apa maksud* plus the word. *Tugasan* means assignment — your phrasebook lists it alongside *kuiz* and *peperiksaan*.
steps.warning: Substituting an English word for the Malay one defeats the exercise. Ask about the Malay word you heard.
steps.check: You can say what the word means in English without looking it up.

steps.title: Close with Terima kasih
steps.detail_markdown: Say **Terima kasih** when you have your answer. It tells the tutor the problem is solved and the class can move on.
steps.warning: Do not just go quiet: without the thank-you the tutor cannot tell whether you got what you needed.
steps.check: The tutor moves on and you are not dreading the next session.

payload.title: Two students, same lecture, different outcome
payload.markdown:
The tutor says, at speed: *Tugasan kumpulan perlu dihantar sebelum kelas minggu depan.*

**Student A** catches *tugasan*, *kumpulan*, *kelas*, *minggu depan* — enough to guess there is a group assignment due next week. She nods. She does not know whether it is before the class or after, does not know the group, and does not know what *dihantar* means. She finds out on the due date that it had to be submitted online by 5pm on Sunday.

**Student B** raises a hand and says:

> Minta maaf. Saya tak faham. Boleh cakap perlahan sikit?

The tutor repeats it slower. B still misses *dihantar*. So:

> Apa maksud "dihantar"?

The tutor says *submit* and adds, in English, that it goes through the portal. B writes it down.

Same class. A leaves with a guess. B leaves with a deadline, a meaning and a submission method — and the tutor now knows B's name and that B asks.

payload.markdown:
BMK 2 is not a phrasebook. It is a module on your degree record, and it has a code, a credit value and a category, the same way your programme's other modules do.

**Module code: MPU31002.** That is the code to look for when you register and on your timetable. Learn it as a string, not as a description.

**2 credits.** It carries two credits toward your degree. Two credits sounds small, which is exactly why it is easy to treat as optional. It is not optional: MPU modules are compulsory, and Taylor's says students must take all the MPU modules listed under each category.

**It sits in the MPU group.** MPU (*Mata Pelajaran Pengajian Umum*) modules are the compulsory general-studies modules of Malaysian higher education, taken alongside your programme. They are not a Taylor's invention and not a language-school add-on: they are a national requirement that Taylor's delivers.

**Taylor's groups MPU modules into categories U1 to U4.** For international degree students, BMK 2 sits in U1, next to *Kursus Integriti dan Antirasuah* and *Citra Malaysia*. Malaysian students take different U1 modules instead of BMK 2, so your BMK class is made up of international students like you.

The practical consequence: BMK 2 is assessed. Your phrasebook is not. Use the phrasebook to survive the mamak, the Grab and the campus — and use it to arrive at BMK 2 already able to say something. Then let the module itself tell you what it assesses.

lessons.title: Capstone: a full day in Malay
lessons.summary: You will spend one real day doing three things in Malay: ordering at a mamak, taking a Grab and holding one conversation on campus. Covers writing your phrases out beforehand, going out and using them, and logging which lines you had to abandon for English. Prevents staying in English for the rest of the year because the first attempt felt clumsy.

payload.markdown:
You have the phrases. What you do not have is a day where you used them.

The failure mode this capstone prevents is specific. You order at a mamak in English, it works, and you conclude that Malay is optional. Six months later you still cannot say *teh tarik kurang manis, satu* without rehearsing it in your head first. The first attempt will feel clumsy. Clumsy is the point.

Today you run three scenes from your phrasebook in one short day:

1. **Mamak breakfast** — order a drink and food, ask for the bill.
2. **Grab ride to campus** — greet the driver, confirm the destination, thank them.
3. **One conversation on campus** — introduce yourself, ask one real question.

Before you leave, write your lines down. Not because you will read them, but because writing them commits you to a specific sentence instead of a vague intention. Use only the phrases from your phrasebook — *teh tarik kurang manis, satu*, *roti canai satu, kuah campur*, *bang, kira*, *terima kasih, bang* — spelled as your phrasebook spells them.

After each scene, log one line: which Malay phrase you actually said, and which one you abandoned for English. The abandoned ones are your real syllabus for next week.

Your phrasebook notes that final *k* is a short stop in the throat, not a full "k" — *tidak* sounds like "tida'". Say your lines out loud once before you go. Stress is light and fairly even, so do not hunt for an English-style emphasis.

payload.intro: Fifteen minutes of preparation, then you go. Do this the evening before or the morning of — not in the queue.

steps.title: Pick your three scenes and write the lines
steps.detail_markdown:
On paper or in your notes app, write three headings: **Mamak**, **Grab**, **Campus**. Under each, write the exact Malay lines you intend to say, copied from your phrasebook.

Mamak, from section 5: *Teh tarik kurang manis, satu.* Then *Roti canai satu, kuah campur.* Then, at the end, *Bang, kira.*

Grab, from section 6: *Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus.* as you get in, then *Terima kasih, bang* on arrival.

Campus, from section 7: *Saya pelajar antarabangsa.* Then one question — *Di mana perpustakaan?* or *Boleh saya duduk di sini?*
steps.warning: Do not write a sentence your phrasebook does not contain. An invented sentence is the one you will freeze on.
steps.check: Three headings, each with at least two Malay lines written out in full.

steps.title: Say every line out loud twice
steps.detail_markdown:
Read each line aloud. Twice. Your phrasebook notes that final *k* is a short stop in the throat, not a full "k" — so *tidak* comes out like "tida'". Stress is light and fairly even; many speakers lean slightly on the second-last syllable.

Say *terima kasih, bang* until the *bang* does not sound like the English word "bang".
steps.check: You can say *Roti canai satu, kuah campur* without looking at the paper.

steps.title: Order at the mamak
steps.detail_markdown:
The waiter will ask *Nak minum apa?* — what would you like to drink. Answer with your written line: *Teh tarik kurang manis, satu.*

They will then ask *Makan?* — anything to eat. Answer: *Roti canai satu, kuah campur.*

When you are done, get attention and say *Bang, kira.* They will name the price, e.g. *Empat ringgit lima puluh sen* — RM 4.50. Pay, then *Terima kasih, bang!*
steps.warning: If they reply faster than you can follow, say the line anyway. You are not being tested on comprehension today.
steps.check: You said at least two Malay lines and the bill arrived.

steps.title: Take the Grab and use your Malay lines
steps.detail_markdown: Get in and say *Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus.* When you are close, *Tolong berhenti di sini.* On arrival, *Terima kasih, bang.* Even one of these lines, said out loud to a real person, counts.
steps.warning: Do not let the app's English interface talk you out of saying the line. The app is not the conversation.
steps.check: *Terima kasih, bang* left your mouth, not just your head.

steps.title: One campus conversation
steps.detail_markdown:
Find one person — classmate, staff, anyone — and say *Saya pelajar antarabangsa.* Then ask your one question: *Di mana perpustakaan?* or *Boleh saya duduk di sini?*

If they answer in English, that is fine. You still opened in Malay.
steps.check: You said the introduction line to a person, not to a mirror.

steps.title: Log what you abandoned
steps.detail_markdown: Within an hour of finishing, write three short entries: scene, phrase you said, phrase you dropped for English. Be honest — the dropped ones are the ones you will drill next week.
steps.check: Three entries, at least one of which names a phrase you did not manage.

payload.title: One day, three scenes, one log
payload.brief_markdown:
Run the day described in this lesson: mamak breakfast, Grab ride to campus, one campus conversation. Then write it up.

**Constraints**
- Every Malay line you report must appear in your phrasebook, spelled as your phrasebook spells it. Do not invent sentences.
- The day must include all three scenes. A day with only the mamak does not count.
- Report what actually happened, including the lines you abandoned. A log with no abandoned lines is almost certainly not honest.

**What "done" looks like**
A short written log with three sections — one per scene. Each section names the Malay lines you said, the lines you dropped for English, and one sentence on what you would say differently next time. Finish with a three-line list of the phrases you are drilling next week.

This fits in one 15-minute sitting after the day itself: the day takes the time, the write-up takes the sitting.
deliverables: A three-section log (mamak, Grab, campus) naming the Malay lines you actually said in each scene.
A list of the phrases you abandoned for English, written out in full.
A three-line drilling list for next week, drawn from the abandoned phrases.
